power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p< .05", Text = "To identify group differences, the resulting clusters were tested for statistical significance (p< .05) using chi-square tests, including post-hoc comparisons (Bortz and Schuster, 2010)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. ownership.dep_title: Why the Mix Matters - Exploring the Dynamics of Polysubstance Use
ownership.dep_description: A widespread form of recreational drug use is known as polysubstance use, which involves consuming two or more psychoactive substances within a short period of time. In addition to the desired effects, such as intensifying or prolonging the high, or counteracting unpleasant effects, polysubstance use also entails risks. To provide polysubstance users with user-centered measures to support health promotion and safer-use, a differentiated understanding of the diverse forms of this consumption practice is required. In an online cross-sectional study, recreational drug users (N= 649) were asked about sociodemographic data and their consumption behavior, with a particular focus on polysubstance use. A hierarchical cluster analysis was performed to identify different types of polysubstance users. The clusters obtained were then tested for diversity using chi-square tests. live_data_statements: Prior to participation, all participants were informed about the study aims and expected duration, as well as the procedures for data processing and storage.
Eligible participants were adults (≥ 18 years) who reported previous or current use of psychoactive substances in recreational settings.
Before taking part in the study, all participants had to actively consent to participate, to data protection, and to the use of their anonymized data for scientific research and publication purposes.
Regarding marital status, 42.8% of participants were single, 35.6% were in a relationship, and 13.7% were married.

Participants were asked about 13 personal consumption rules or rituals, which were grouped into three broader categories due to low frequencies of individual rules: (1) drugrelated, (2) set-related, and (3) setting-related rules (supplementary table 2).

The participants were 31.10 years old on average (SD= 8.54, min.= 18, max.= 58), with the most cis women (n= 74; 57.4%), followed by 32.6% (n= 42) cis men, 8.5% (n= 11) non-binary individuals, and 0.8% (n= 1) other without further details (missing answers: n= 1; 0.8%).
Furthermore, participants were recruited from 22 countries, with the majority residing in Austria, Germany, and Switzerland.
All participants provided written informed consent for the use and publication of their anonymized data.

text.text: Broadly defined, polysubstance use refers to the consumption of two or more psychoactive substances within a short period of time.
In addition to the desired effects, such as intensifying or prolonging the high or counteracting unpleasant effects, polysubstance use also entails risks.
However, much of the existing research on psychoactive substance use continues to focus on single-substance use, leaving the heterogeneity of polysubstance use comparatively less understood.
A differentiated understanding of these patterns is therefore needed to inform user-centered approaches to health promotion and safer use.

In an online cross-sectional study, people who consume psychoactive substances in recreational settings (N= 649; Mage= 32.09) provided information on sociodemographic characteristics and substance use patterns, with a particular focus on polysubstance use.
Hierarchical cluster analysis identified distinct patterns of polysubstance use, followed by chi-square tests to examine group differences.

Three distinct clusters (Cluster 1: n= 182; Cluster 2: n= 129; Cluster 3: n= 137) were identified, differing in polysubstance use patterns, underlying motivations, and engagement in substance use management practices.
The findings highlight that people who engage in polysubstance use constitute a heterogeneous population with distinct patterns of use and related behaviors.
Recognizing this heterogeneity should help to support the development of more targeted, user-centered approaches for safer use and health promotion.

So-called psychoactive substance use in recreational settings, defined as the controlled and planned consumption of legal and illegal psychoactive substances during leisure time and in specific social situations (Pol and Hawks, 1992), does not necessarily imply problematic use or a substance use disorder.

text.text: At the same time, recreational patterns of substance use remain relevant from a public health and clinical perspective, particularly in the context of polysubstance use.
The risks associated with the consumption of psychoactive substances in leisure settings are often due to the predominantly illegal status of psychoactive substances.

Possession and use may lead to stigmatization, pathologization, and legal consequences, prohibition creates uncertainty about substance origin and composition, increasing the risk of unintended overdoses, unexpected substances, and other health-related harms (EMCDDA, 2021).

text.text: A widely observed practice of substance use is polysubstance use (PSU), which is increasingly considered a public health issue, as the simultaneous use of different substances may be associated with an increased risk of overdose, substance use disorder, and adverse drug interactions (Boileau-Falardeau et al., 2022; Crummy, 2020; EMCDDA, 2021; Fleury et al., 2026; Grov et al., 2009; LeComte et al., 2025; Reichenberger et al., 2026; Rodzlan Hasani et al., 2023; Rough and Nader, 2026).

text.text: Importantly, the specific substances combined may be associated with distinct health risks and pharmacological interactions.

For example, combining opioids and benzodiazepines increases the risk of respiratory depression (Sun et al., 2017), while the combined use of cocaine and alcohol is associated with increased cardiotoxicity compared to either substance alone (Crummy et al., 2020).

text.text: Non-medical use of prescription medications is also relevant in the context of PSU, with previous studies identifying distinct consumption patterns involving combinations with cannabis, alcohol, and other prescription medications (Rockhill et al., 2025; Steinhoff et al., 2022).

text.text: Overall, these findings highlight the importance of considering the diversity of substance combinations and their associated risks when examining PSU and developing targeted harm reduction strategies.

Various studies of people who use psychoactive substances in recreational settings have reported PSU prevalence rates of 70-94%, depending on the study design, the precise definition of PSU, and substance groups examined (Schauer et al., 2015; Schlienz and Lee, 2018; Stetina et al., 2008; Uhl and Stetina, 2025).

text.text: Young adulthood represents a particularly relevant developmental period for substance use and PSU.
This stage of life is often characterized by increased autonomy, identity exploration, and experimentation with different behaviors, including substance use (Arnett, 2000).

text.text: Substance use also tends to peak during young adulthood, although peak ages vary across substance classes (Schulenberg et al., 2020; Stevens et al., 2022).

text.text: In broad terms, PSU refers to the use of two or more psychoactive substances.
However, PSU is not uniformly defined, as reflected by the variety of terms used in the literature, including "polydrug use", "co-use", "simultaneous use", "concurrent use", or "mixed use".

Studies assessing the use of different psychoactive substances over broader reference periods, such as the past 12 months, do not necessarily capture whether these substances were consumed simultaneously or whether their effects overlapped.
The different concepts used to describe PSU primarily differ in terms of the timing of substance use (Bunting et al., 2024; EMCDDA, 2021; Grov et al., 2009).

text.text: Current research commonly distinguishes between simultaneous and concurrent use.

Simultaneous use refers to the use of two or more psychoactive substances at the same time or within a short period during the same occasion, such that their effects overlap (Baggio et al., 2014; Foxx et al., 2022; Parthasarathy et al., 2025; Quek et al., 2013).

text.text: In contrast, concurrent use refers to the use of multiple substances within a broader specified reference period (Fleury et al., 2026; Parthasarathy et al., 2025), such as the past 30 days (Foxx et al., 2022) or 12 months (Baggio et al., 2014; Quek et al., 2013), without necessarily involving overlapping effects.

text.text: The timing and sequence of PSU may be closely related to the intended effects, illustrating the close connection between PSU (what is taken and when) and the underlying motives (why it is taken).
The variety of terms and inconsistent definitions of PSU have important implications for empirical research, as they limit comparability across studies.

Moreover, conceptual ambiguity may complicate the development and implementation of support strategies and health promotion measures in general by making it less clear "what to target" (e.g., Bunting et al., 2024).

text.text: In the present study, PSU is defined as simultaneous use, referring to the use of two or more psychoactive substances at the same time or within a short period during a particular occasion such that their effects overlap.

This definition is also consistent with Rough and Nader (2026), who argue that PSU should capture temporally proximal patterns of substance use rather than the use of different substances across periods of several weeks or months.

text.text: While the literature describes common motives, the specific combination and importance of these motives remain highly individual.

Consequently, a holistic understanding of PSU requires consideration not only of the substances used in combination and their temporal sequence, but also the motivations underlying the combined use (Bunting et al., 2024; Fleury et al., 2026; Grov et al., 2009).

text.text: Consumption-related behaviors such as drugchecking, self-defined consumption rules, and the use of professional support services may therefore provide an additional perspective on how individuals manage their PSU.

For example, drug-checking services provide information about substance composition and may influence consumption decisions, particularly when unexpected substances are detected (Betzler et al., 2021; EMCDDA, 2021).

text.text: However, to our knowledge, comparatively less attention has been paid to identifying heterogeneous patterns of PSU in recreational settings by jointly considering substance combinations, motives for mixed use, and substance use management practices, such as drugchecking, professional support service use, and adherence to self-defined consumption rules.
Considering these different dimensions together may contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of PSU.
Such an approach may help inform tailored harm reduction strategies and drug literacy initiatives (Gerlach, 2004).

text.text: This study therefore examines patterns of PSU among people who use psychoactive substances in recreational settings to identify distinct consumption types and contribute to a more nuanced understanding of this heterogeneous phenomenon.

In an exploratory open online cross-sectional study, people who use psychoactive substances in leisure settings were asked about their use of both legal and illegal psychoactive substances.
Individuals who use psychoactive substances in recreational settings are often considered a hard-to-reach population in research.

Owing to the predominantly prohibitive legal and social context surrounding the use of illicit substances, many individuals prefer to remain anonymous and avoid disclosing their substance use, contributing to their characterization as a hidden population.

Current studies in this context rely on online surveys, as this form of questioning offers a high degree of anonymity and is therefore well suited to reaching this hidden population (Miller and Sønderlund, 2018; Stetina et al., 2008; Stetina and Kryspin-Exner, 2009).

text.text: The survey was distributed in collaboration with partners from the fields of drug-checking, music and techno collectives, and scene-specific internet and social media platforms, who shared the study link and flyers (supplemental figure 1) with the community.

An online questionnaire specifically developed for the present study was used to collect data, which, in addition to sociodemographic data such as age, gender, or educational status, collected aspects of general consumption behavior like the 1-year prevalence or the use of drug-checking, as well as characteristics of PSU (for example, combined substances, frequency, motives).

All items were developed and formulated by the research team, with their content informed by a broad review of relevant empirical studies and epidemiological prevalence reports (Infodrog Swiss Coordination and Expert Center for Addiction, 2023; European Union Drugs Agency, 2025; EMCDDA, 2021; Boileau-Falardeau et al., 2022; Greń et al., 2024; Hughes et al., 2019; Gabrovec et al., 2023; Kruger et al., 2023; National Harm Reduction Coalition, 2020).

The aim of the study was to explore patterns of PSU and identify distinct types of consumption within this heterogeneous practice.

Building on the research gap outlined in the Introduction, particularly the limited evidence on PSU patterns jointly considering substance combinations, motives for mixed use, and substance use management practices in recreational settings, an exploratory approach was adopted.
Accordingly, no specific a priori hypotheses regarding the number or characteristics of the resulting clusters were formulated.
Research question: What distinct consumption types can be identified within polysubstance use?
Eligible participants were adults (≥ 18 years) who reported previous or current use of psychoactive substances in recreational settings.
To facilitate international participation, the questionnaire was provided in both German and English.
No financial or other incentives were offered for participation.
Before taking part in the study, all participants had to actively consent to participate, to data protection, and to the use of their anonymized data for scientific research and publication purposes.
Statistical calculations were performed using the SPSS 29 statistics program (IBM Corp., 2022, Armonk, NY, USA).
All participants with valid data for the respective variables were included in the analyses whenever possible.
Missing responses were coded as missing values in SPSS (Leiner, 2019) and reported alongside the corresponding results.

text.text: No imputation of missing data was performed.
Frequency analyses for descriptive sample descriptions were presented based on mean values (M) and standard deviations (SD).
Frequency tables and histograms were used for graphical illustration.
Since rounding may occur during descriptive calculations using the statistics program, the percentages may deviate slightly from 100% (Bortz and Schuster, 2010).

text.text: To reflect the diversity of PSU, questions were asked not only about the existence of this consumption practice and the combined substances, but also about its frequency.

As Fleury et al. (2026), like Bunting and colleagues (2024), emphasize, assessing the three dimensions of (1) the number and type of substances combined, (2) the timing of substance use, and (3) the intention underlying their use is essential for a comprehensive assessment of PSU.
text.formatted: As <ref type="formula">Fleury et al. (2026), like Bunting and colleagues (2024)</ref>, emphasize, assessing the three dimensions of (1) the number and type of substances combined, (2) the timing of substance use, and (3) the intention underlying their use is essential for a comprehensive assessment of PSU.

text.text: Frequency was assessed using a scale of nine frequency categories (ranging from once a year to several times a day).

To represent the frequency of PSU, the predefined response categories were grouped into three frequency levels: (1) low-frequency PSU (ranging from once a year to several times within six months), (2) moderate-frequency PSU (ranging from once a month to once a week), and (3) high-frequency PSU (ranging from several times a week to several times a day) (supplemental table 2).
Because substance combinations and underlying motives exhibit a high degree of individuality, both were assessed using open-ended questions.
Open-ended responses allowed participants to report their individual substance combinations and subjective motivations without being restricted to predefined response categories.

These questions provide particularly informative added value, especially when it comes to exploratory topics or the determination of cognitions and attitudes and were therefore considered the most appropriate approach (Hansen and Świderska, 2024; Möhring and Schlütz, 2019).
text.formatted: These questions provide particularly informative added value, especially when it comes to exploratory topics or the determination of cognitions and attitudes and were therefore considered the most appropriate approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hansen and Świderska, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Möhring and Schlütz, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: To analyze substance combinations, the reported substances were grouped into broader categories, as the large number of individual combinations (N = 556) resulted in frequencies that were too small for statistical analysis.

First, each reported substance was classified according to its predominant effects as a stimulant (upper; e.g., amphetamine, cocaine), depressant (downer; e.g., benzodiazepines, cannabidiol [CBD]), or hallucinogen/dissociative (e.g., tetrahydrocannabinol [THC], ketamine).
The complete classification of all reported substances into these three categories is provided in Supplemental Table 3.
text.formatted: The complete classification of all reported substances into these three categories is provided in Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">3</ref>.

text.text: However, the complexity of such a classification must be acknowledged, as the predominant effects of individual substances may vary depending on factors such as dosage (e.g., gamma-hydroxybutyrate [GHB] may produce euphoric effects at lower doses and predominantly depressant effects at higher doses).

Nevertheless, substances were classified according to their predominant pharmacological effects to provide a consistent framework for grouping the large variety of reported combinations and enable subsequent statistical analyses.

Based on these classifications, the reported substance combinations were subsequently assigned to one of six combination groups (upper + upper, downer + downer, hallucinogens/dissociatives + hallucinogens/dissociatives, upper + downer, upper + hallucinogens/dissociative, downer + hallucinogens/dissociatives).
To analyse the motives behind PSU, the motivation categories were developed based on participants' open-ended responses and subsequently grouped into broader conceptual categories.

Although previous studies have proposed more differentiated motivational frameworks (Boileau-Falardeau, 2022; EMCDDA, 2009; Fleury et al., 2026; Grov et al., 2009; Kataja et al., 2017; Reichenberger et al., 2026), Rough and Nader (2026) describe positive and negative reinforcement as key mechanisms underlying PSU, whereby substances may be combined either to enhance desired effects or to reduce unpleasant effects associated with another substance.

text.text: Furthermore, the present study used broader motivational categories to enable systematic classification of open-ended responses and ensure sufficient frequencies for subsequent statistical analyses.

Two motive classes were formed based on current research studies and theoretical considerations: (1) counteract effects (e.g., to promote sleep; to mitigate undesirable/unpleasant effects of other substances), (2) enhance (e.g., to intensify effect profiles or achieve new effects; to prolong the high).
Analysis of the responses revealed two notable features.
Firstly, some participants reported "unintentional" or "inevitable" PSU.

This was the case when the person was either receiving pharmacological treatment (e.g., attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder [ADHD], opioid painkillers), experiencing substance dependence (mostly nicotine), or consuming substances as part of the same administration practice (such as smoking cannabis together with tobacco).

Given that PSU involving nicotine, alcohol, or cannabis is often overlooked or excluded from research despite its high prevalence and potentially enhancing effects, this motive warrants particular consideration (Bunting et al., 2024; Connor et al., 2023; Fleury et al., 2026; Goodhines et al., 2025; Graupensperger et al., 2024; Reichenberger et al., 2026).

text.text: Since mixed consumption was "inevitable" in these cases, the category of structurally induced PSU was introduced.
In contrast, the analysis of consumption motives showed that many participants stated they engaged in PSU "without any particular reason" and "without thinking".
From this, the consumption motivation of situational PSU without an explicit motive was derived.
To identify distinct PSU groups, we performed a hierarchical cluster analysis.

This exploratory approach was chosen because it groups individuals with similar patterns across multiple characteristics without requiring the number or structure of clusters to be specified a priori.
Ward's method was applied to obtain relatively homogeneous clusters by minimizing within-cluster variance, using squared Euclidean distance as the distance measure (Fromm, 2010; Hair et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Ward's method was applied to obtain relatively homogeneous clusters by minimizing within-cluster variance, using squared Euclidean distance as the distance measure <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Fromm, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Hair et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Variables used to form clusters included polysubstance use (yes/no), the substance groups combined, motives for mixed use, and behavioral factors, including drug-checking (yes/no), use of professional support services (yes/no), and adherence to selfdefined consumption rules.
To identify group differences, the resulting clusters were tested for statistical significance (p< .05) using chi-square tests, including post-hoc comparisons (Bortz and Schuster, 2010).

text.text: At the first data cut-off in November 2025, the study included 649 participants, with a mean age of 32.09 years (SD= 10.34; range= 18-74).
Among participants with available age data (n = 582), 49.0% were aged 18-29 years, 37.5% were aged 30-44 years, and 13.6% 45 years and older.
Cis women represented the largest gender group (52.5%), followed by cis men (38.2%).
The sample covered 22 countries, although participation was concentrated in Austria (45.5%), Germany (22%), and Switzerland (6.8%).
Heterosexual orientation was most frequently reported (63%), while bisexual (13.7%) and pansexual (10%) orientations represented the next largest groups.
Regarding marital status, 42.8% of participants were single, 35.6% were in a relationship, and 13.7% were married.
Approximately one in five participants reported having children (19.3%).
Living arrangements were diverse, with living with a partner (27.9%) and living alone (27.6%) being the most common.
More than half of the participants held a university or college degree (51.8%), while 20.3% reported a high school diploma as their highest educational qualification.
A complete description of the sample is provided in table 1.

text.text: Past-year substance use covered a broad range of psychoactive substances.
Alcohol (85.4%), tobacco (61.6%), and THC (56.4%) were reported most frequently, followed by CBD (37.8%), MDMA (34.2%), cocaine (31%), and amphetamine (24%).
Several other substances were reported at lower prevalence rates, illustrating the diversity of substances used within the sample.
Prevalence rates for all assessed substances are presented in figure 1.

text.text: Participants were asked about 13 personal consumption rules or rituals, which were grouped into three broader categories due to low frequencies of individual rules: (1) drugrelated, (2) set-related, and (3) setting-related rules (supplementary table 2).
Overall, adherence was high across all three categories, with set-related rules reported most frequently (60.6%), followed by setting-related (57.3%) and drug-related rules (54.2%).

The use of drug-checking services was reported by 38.5% of participants (30.2% missing), whereas 10.2% reported having used professional support services related to their substance use (22.3% missing) (table 2).
A total of 404 participants (62.2%) reported having used two or more substances simultaneously or in quick succession.

To characterize patterns of PSU, open-ended responses on substance combinations were assigned to broader substance classes.

Across 556 reported combinations, upper + upper (n= 230) and upper + hallucinogen/dissociative (n= 222) were most frequently reported, followed by hallucinogen/dissociative + hallucinogen/dissociative combinations (n= 67).
To examine motives for PSU, open-ended responses were assigned to four motive categories as described in section 2.5.

Across 446 responses, enhancement motives were most frequently reported (n= 191), followed by situational PSU without an explicit motive (n= 128), counteracting effects (n= 90), and structurally induced PSU (n= 37) (table 2).
After performing a hierarchical cluster analysis, a 3-cluster solution proved to be the most plausible.
The substance combination groups downer + downer, downer + hallucinogens/dissociatives, and upper + downer were excluded from the chi-square tests due to expected cell frequencies (n≤ 5).
Cluster 1 was the largest cluster with 182 participants, an average age of 32.74 years (SD= 10.31, min.= 18, max.= 68) and with slightly more cis men (n= 86; 47.3%) than cis women (n= 78;42.9 %).
Then followed by 5.5% (n= 10) non-binary persons, 1.6% (n= 3) genderfluid persons, 1.1% (n= 2) trans*women, and 1.1% (n= 2) other without further specification (missing answers: n= 1; 0.5%).

All participants from cluster 1 (n= 182; 58.3%) reported PSU, in which all substance combinations [upper + upper (n= 97; 49.5%), hallucinogens/dissociatives + hallucinogens/dissociatives (n= 50; 89.3%), uppers + hallucinogens/dissociatives (n= 131; 68.6%)] were consumed significantly more frequently than expected.
The motives counteract effects (n= 78; 94%) and enhance (n= 148; 87.6%) were mentioned significantly more often.
Situational PSU without an explicit motive (n= 17; 16.2%) occurred significantly less often.
People in cluster 1 made above-average use of professional support services (n= 35; 63.6%) and drug-checking (n= 139; 56.5%).
Compliance with consumption rules regarding drug (n= 152; 44.3%) and set (n= 171; 44.6%) was significantly more frequent (table 3).
Cluster 2 was the smallest cluster with n= 129.

The participants were 31.10 years old on average (SD= 8.54, min.= 18, max.= 58), with the most cis women (n= 74; 57.4%), followed by 32.6% (n= 42) cis men, 8.5% (n= 11) non-binary individuals, and 0.8% (n= 1) other without further details (missing answers: n= 1; 0.8%).
In cluster 2, all participants except one reported PSU (n= 128; 41%).
The combination of the substance groups upper + upper (n= 99; 50.5%) occurred at a significantly higher frequency than expected.
In contrast, the group hallucinogens/dissociatives + hallucinogens/dissociatives (n= 6; 10.7%) was consumed significantly less frequently.
PSU was found more frequently than average in situational contexts, without any explicit motive (n= 88; 83.8%), and for structural reasons (n= 16; 50%).
The motives of counteracting effects (n= 5; 6%) and enhancement (n= 21; 12.4%) played a significantly lesser role.

People from cluster 2 showed no significant deviations regarding the use of professional support services (n= 14; 25.5%) and drug-checking (n= 67; 27.2%), nor about consumption rules in the areas of drug (n= 94; 27.4%) and set (n= 108; 28.2%) (table 3).

text.text: The identified heterogeneity in polysubstance use has important implications for prevention and health promotion.

In cluster 1, the second-oldest cluster, all participants reported PSU, characterized by a broad range of substance combinations and predominantly targeted motivations such as minimizing unpleasant effects, enhancing pleasant effects, or creating new effects.

This pattern is consistent with previous research showing that PSU may involve intentional substance combinations aimed at enhancing, modifying, or counteracting specific effects (Boileau-Falardeau et al., 2022; Grov et al., 2009; Lake and Lucas, 2024; Rodzlan Hasani et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with previous research showing that PSU may involve intentional substance combinations aimed at enhancing, modifying, or counteracting specific effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Boileau-Falardeau et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Grov et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Lake and Lucas, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Rodzlan Hasani et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Cluster 1 also constituted the largest polysubstance group in the present study, paralleling findings by Parthasarathy et al. (2025), who identified simultaneous PSU as the largest of three distinct PSU-groups.
text.formatted: Cluster 1 also constituted the largest polysubstance group in the present study, paralleling findings by <ref type="bibr">Parthasarathy et al. (2025)</ref>, who identified simultaneous PSU as the largest of three distinct PSU-groups.

text.text: Importantly, participants in cluster 1 also reported greater use of drug-checking, professional support services, and self-defined consumption rules.
Taken together, these characteristics suggest that frequent and targeted PSU may coexist with greater engagement in self-regulatory practices and available support services.

A similar pattern was observed by Greń et al. (2024), whose profile 5 combined a broad range of substances with contextspecific intentions, while showing the lowest health risks and greater use of protective behavioral strategies compared with other profiles.
text.formatted: A similar pattern was observed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Greń et al. (2024)</ref>, whose profile 5 combined a broad range of substances with contextspecific intentions, while showing the lowest health risks and greater use of protective behavioral strategies compared with other profiles.

text.text: The authors suggested that these strategies may partly explain the relatively limited negative outcomes despite intensive PSU.

Drugchecking services and related support measures, including counselling and educational interventions, represent important components of health promotion for people who use psychoactive substances in recreational settings and have been shown to be well accepted (Barsch, 2004; Betzler et al., 2021; Grace Rose et al., 2023; Hirschfeld et al., 2024; Karden et al., 2025).

text.text: However, barriers such as inconvenient locations or limited opening hours, long waiting times, concerns about anonymity, and fear of police involvement may limit their regular use (Aronson et al., 2024; Grace Rose et al., 2023; Karden et al., 2025; Sande and Šabić, 2018).

text.text: The characteristics of cluster 1 therefore suggest that increasing the availability and accessibility of drug-checking, low-threshold educational, and counselling services may be particularly relevant for individuals showing this pattern of PSU.
Cluster 2 was the youngest and smallest cluster.
Although all but one participant reported pronounced PSU, this cluster differed from cluster 1 in terms of substance combinations, underlying motivations, and substance use management practices.
In addition to the predominant consumption of stimulant combinations, PSU was more often spontaneous or opportunistic rather than motivated by specific intended effects.

In this context, Fleury et al. (2026) emphasize the importance of considering the intention underlying PSU when developing interventions and health promotion measures, as unintentional or opportunistic PSU, for example due to availability, social factors, habitual use, or accidental co-use, may require different preventive approaches than intentional PSU aimed at enhancing desired effects.
text.formatted: In this context, <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Fleury et al. (2026)</ref> emphasize the importance of considering the intention underlying PSU when developing interventions and health promotion measures, as unintentional or opportunistic PSU, for example due to availability, social factors, habitual use, or accidental co-use, may require different preventive approaches than intentional PSU aimed at enhancing desired effects.

text.text: Furthermore, cluster 2 was characterized by a significantly lower use of self-defined consumption rules, professional support services, and drug-checking.

Given the more spontaneous and opportunistic pattern observed in this cluster, services that require prior planning or involve delays may be less compatible with the circumstances in which PSU occurs.

This interpretation is supported by recent research identifying limited availability and relatively long waiting times for test results as key barriers to the uptake of counselling and drug-checking services (Eide et al., 2024; Karden et al., 2025; Maghsoudi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This interpretation is supported by recent research identifying limited availability and relatively long waiting times for test results as key barriers to the uptake of counselling and drug-checking services <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Eide et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Karden et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Maghsoudi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Low-threshold and readily accessible approaches to providing evidence-based information may therefore be particularly relevant for reaching individuals with this pattern of PSU and supporting informed decision-making.
However, the reasons for the lower use of substance use management practices cannot be determined from the present data.

Whether this reflects limited awareness or accessibility of such services, lower perceived relevance, or problematic assumptions about the substances being used (e.g., the belief that one is in possession of particularly "pure" or "harmless" substances) requires further investigation.
A better understanding of these factors could help tailor information and support services to this subgroup's specific characteristics.
Only two participants in cluster 3, which was characterized by the highest mean age and the largest proportion of cis women, reported PSU.

This finding is broadly consistent with epidemiological research indicating associations of PSU with younger age and male gender (De Jonge et al., 2022; Rodzlan Hasani et al., 2023; Stevens et al., 2022; Tucker et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This finding is broadly consistent with epidemiological research indicating associations of PSU with younger age and male gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(De Jonge et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Rodzlan Hasani et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Stevens et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Tucker et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Cluster 3 was also characterized by significantly lower engagement in substance use management practices, including drug-checking, professional support services, and selfdefined consumption rules.

However, because of the cross-sectional design, it remains unclear whether this lower engagement reflects the absence of PSU or whether the identified clusters represent different patterns along a broader PSU continuum.
Moreover, the absence of current PSU does not necessarily imply that such patterns remain stable over time.
As reflected in cluster 2, PSU may occur spontaneously or situationally.
In addition, unexpected psychoactive substances or adulterants may result in unintentional or unrecognized PSU (Palamar et al., 2021; Peck et al., 2019; Sevigny et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In addition, unexpected psychoactive substances or adulterants may result in unintentional or unrecognized PSU <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Palamar et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Peck et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Sevigny et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: From a harm-reduction perspective, which is preventive rather than reactive, early education and providing accessible information before such patterns emerge may therefore support informed decision-making.
To sum up, this study identified three distinct patterns of substance use, highlighting the heterogeneity of PSU.

Previous research has also reported a three-group structure, commonly distinguishing between limited-range, moderate-range, and extended-range PSU based on the breadth of substances involved (Stevens et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Previous research has also reported a three-group structure, commonly distinguishing between limited-range, moderate-range, and extended-range PSU based on the breadth of substances involved <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Stevens et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This complexity among people who use psychoactive substances and their consumption practices underscores the need to tailor measures promoting safer-use initiatives and health promotion to different subgroups.

In this context, the understanding of harm reduction should be broadened, as Fleury et al. (2026) emphasize that harms associated with PSU extend beyond overdose and may also include social exclusion, school disciplinary consequences, and criminalization.

(2026)</ref> emphasize that harms associated with PSU extend beyond overdose and may also include social exclusion, school disciplinary consequences, and criminalization.

text.text: By providing accessible, evidence-based information and support, such approaches may strengthen drug literacy and facilitate informed decision-making.
The use of psychoactive substances in recreational settings repeatedly poses numerous obstacles to empirical research.

The pathologizing and stigmatizing public discourse surrounding this topic marginalizes individuals who use such substances, which contributes significantly to the difficulty of reaching this hidden population (Stetina et al., 2008).

text.text: The convenience sample collected in this study may therefore be representative of people with a use of psychoactive substances in leisure settings but cannot claim to be representative of the general population.
To account for individual characteristics, participants reported the substances combined in PSU, as well as the underlying motivation, using an open-ended response format.
This resulted in around 190 different substance combinations and over 640 motivations, some of which were mentioned only very rarely.
Because small sample groups can distort effects (Bortz and Schuster, 2010; Möhring and Schlütz, 2019), this data were not suitable for statistical calculations.
text.formatted: Because small sample groups can distort effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bortz and Schuster, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Möhring and Schlütz, 2019)</ref>, this data were not suitable for statistical calculations.

text.text: To make statistical statements, nonetheless, the individual mentions had to be assigned to higher-level substance categories.
This enabled statistical calculations but came with a certain loss of information.
In addition, open-ended questions present several challenges during analysis.
Potential sources of error include a lack of clarity and contextual information in written responses, researcher bias as well as translation and coding errors (Scholz et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Potential sources of error include a lack of clarity and contextual information in written responses, researcher bias as well as translation and coding errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Scholz et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This limitation should be considered when interpreting the resulting categories.
Furthermore, participants were recruited from 22 countries, with the majority residing in Austria, Germany, and Switzerland.

Differences in national legal and drug policy frameworks may influence substance use patterns, including the specific substances combined, as changes in the legal status of psychoactive substances can affect substance availability and consumption patterns (Boileau-Falardeau et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Differences in national legal and drug policy frameworks may influence substance use patterns, including the specific substances combined, as changes in the legal status of psychoactive substances can affect substance availability and consumption patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Boileau-Falardeau et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Such differences may also affect access to harm reduction services and participants' willingness to disclose substance use.
As these country-specific contextual factors were not specifically accounted for in the present analyses, their potential influence on the findings remains unclear.
The reliance on self-reported data collected through an online survey represents a further limitation.
Self-reported substance use may be affected by recall bias and social desirability bias (Althubaiti, 2016; Schwarz and Oyserman, 2001).
text.formatted: Self-reported substance use may be affected by recall bias and social desirability bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Althubaiti, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Schwarz and Oyserman, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Previous research comparing self-reported substance use with hair toxicology has also demonstrated underreporting for certain substances, raising concerns about the validity of self-reported consumption patterns (Steinhoff et al., 2023; Janousch et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Previous research comparing self-reported substance use with hair toxicology has also demonstrated underreporting for certain substances, raising concerns about the validity of self-reported consumption patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Steinhoff et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Janousch et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: As no repeated assessment was conducted, the test-retest reliability of the responses could not be evaluated.
Another limitation concerns the cross-sectional design of the present study.
Crosssectional analyses provide a snapshot but cannot capture changes over time (Möhring and Schlütz, 2019; Ullrich, 2018).
text.formatted: Crosssectional analyses provide a snapshot but cannot capture changes over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Möhring and Schlütz, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Ullrich, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Although three distinct patterns of PSU were identified, it remained unclear whether these patterns represent different stages in the development of substance use over time.

For example, it remains unclear whether individuals may transition from predominantly single-substance use (cluster 3) to more spontaneous PSU (cluster 2) and subsequently to more strategic PSU (cluster 1) or whether these clusters represent stable but distinct patterns among different individuals.
Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify whether transitions between clusters occur over time (Möhring and Schlütz, 2019; Ullrich, 2018).
